title: User manual
text:
1. Purpose and workshop route
ADAM-Edu is a browser-based teaching tool for animal breeding and quantitative genetics. It connects population history and linkage disequilibrium (LD), the construction of a base population, and selection and reproduction over breeding years. Use the workshop links supplied by your instructor. You need a computer, a modern web browser and internet access.

Before the workshop
You need a computer, a modern web browser and internet access. No installation, R, programming or participant account is needed. You can use any internet connection; you do not need to share the instructor’s Wi-Fi.

Open the workshop page: https://lhmsai007.shinyapps.io/ADAM-Edu-current/workshop/index.html
Check that all three application buttons open. Save the manual and practical PDFs from that page. You do not need to read the whole manual before class.
Find your browser’s Downloads folder. The applications exchange full population files through Download and Upload controls; separate tabs do not share populations automatically.
Work in pairs. Record or download each result before another run replaces it. Keep the application tab open while a simulation runs.



Workshop quick start
Follow the practical for four short stages: LD and historical diversity (0-4 minutes), base traits and economic values (4-8), breeding methods and donor reproduction (8-25), then a teaching activity (25-30). Begin with LD, then use the prepared history if a new run is slow. Generate B5 and compare E2/E3 for correlated response. The main breeding task then deliberately switches to a separate prepared young-candidate population; it is not a continuation of B5.
In Current population choose Workshop default: BLUP versus GBLUP (young candidates), click Load programme settings, check the schedule and run. Record accuracy, gain, inbreeding and generation interval before changing the donor-reproduction template for the second run. The practical gives the exact settings. Use the prepared reference results if computation would delay discussion. The full manual below is a reference; advanced controls are not prerequisites for the workshop.
The three applications may open in separate tabs. Separate online applications do not automatically share results. Download the full historical population and upload it in Base population; then download the full base population and upload it in Current population. CSV tables and PNG figures are useful records, but do not replace the full-population download for these transfers. Keep the same selected historical scenario and base when making a controlled comparison. A new run replaces the displayed results, so record or download results first.
This manual describes both the prepared examples and the full controls. Beginners can follow the named examples without editing advanced settings. Defaults below refer to the ordinary starting controls; loading a preset can change them. Check the displayed settings and active schedule before running.

title: User manual
text:
2. Historical population: simulation model
This module simulates a finite, diploid population forward through non-overlapping generations. Each animal carries two phased chromosome copies. Founding alleles are sampled independently at marker sites, so markers begin in linkage equilibrium in expectation. Finite sampling can still produce nonzero initial LD.
Each offspring receives a paternal and a maternal gamete. Parents are sampled randomly with replacement from the male and female populations. Gametes inherit chromosome segments with Haldane recombination: for adjacent markers separated by d Morgans, the probability of a phase switch is (1 - exp(-2d))/2. Genetic map distance controls recombination. Physical distance provides marker coordinates; changing Mb alone does not change recombination.
Mutation flips 0 to 1 or 1 to 0 at existing biallelic marker sites. It does not create new sites. Demographic histories change the numbers of breeding males and females, producing drift, changes in diversity and LD. There is no selection or migration in this historical module. The examples illustrate mechanisms and are not a calibrated cattle population or a mutation-drift equilibrium model.

Genome and initial population parameters








Control
Starting value / options
Meaning and effect




Quick-start settings; Load these defaults
Teaching defaults or larger marker set
Loads a group of settings. The larger preset uses 5,000 SNPs per chromosome and a shorter history; it is not simply a higher-resolution version of an otherwise identical run. Inspect settings after loading.


Chromosomes
3; 1-12
Number of independently inherited chromosomes.


Initial males; Initial females
40; 40
Census counts at generation 0. Each sex needs at least two animals; total historical population cannot exceed 500. These are not effective population sizes.


SNPs per chromosome
1,000
Number of biallelic marker sites. Enter one value for every chromosome or comma-separated values in chromosome order. Up to 5,000 per chromosome and 60,000 overall. More markers increase computation and can improve resolution.


Chromosome length (cM)
100
Genetic map length. One value can apply to all chromosomes. More cM generally gives more recombination. 100 cM equals one Morgan.


Physical length (Mb)
100
Physical coordinate span. One Mb is one million base pairs. This sets positions, not the crossover rate.


SNP positions / locations
Even, Random, Clustered
Even spacing, sorted random positions, or groups around sampled centres. Marker distribution changes the distances represented in LD bins.


Optional custom marker map (.csv)
Optional
Uploaded table with chr, position_cm and position_bp; snp is optional. It overrides chromosome number, marker counts, lengths and location settings. Each chromosome needs at least three markers with strictly increasing genetic and physical positions; marker names must be unique.


LD pair sample budget
30,000; 100-200,000
Approximate within-chromosome pair budget. Small examples use all pairs; large examples sample pairs. More pairs reduce pair-sampling noise but require more time. This is not the number of animals.





Allele frequencies and run parameters








Control
Starting value / options
Meaning and effect




Starting allele-frequency distribution
Uniform MAF
Uniform MAF samples initial allele probabilities between the minimum and 0.5. Equal (0.5) uses 0.5 at every site. Rare-enriched MAF favours low frequencies. Fixed frequency assigns one specified probability to every site. All ancestral (0) begins with no segregating sites.


Min. initial MAF
0.05
Lower bound for Uniform MAF and Rare-enriched MAF. It does not force each realized founder-sample frequency to exceed that bound. It does not filter later generations.


Fixed freq. (when selected)
0.2
Starting probability of allele 1 under Fixed frequency. It can range from 0 to 1. Not used by the other frequency modes.


Generations
30; 1-120
Number of historical generations after generation 0.


Random seed
2026
Controls random draws. Repeat the same complete configuration and seed for reproducibility; changing a setting can change subsequent random draws.


Mutation per SNP / gamete
0.00001; 0-0.1
Probability of an allele flip at each transmitted site. Each scenario multiplies this shared rate by its own multiplier. The resulting rate must remain valid. High illustrative rates are not realistic estimates for every species.


LD distance bin (cM)
5; 0.2-50
Width of distance groups in the LD plot. Narrow bins reveal detail but can contain few pairs; wider bins smooth the pattern.


Independent historical replicates
5; 1-100
Independent founder genomes and historical realizations. Enabled scenarios share a founder genome within each replicate, giving paired scenario comparisons.


Uncertainty bands
SE, SD, 95% confidence interval, None
SD describes differences across runs. SE = SD/sqrt(n) describes uncertainty in the mean. Confidence intervals use a t distribution. At least two valid runs are needed; bands are pointwise.





Scenario parameters
Up to five scenarios can run together. Their labels describe the displayed comparison; the history type and numerical settings determine the simulation.







Control
Meaning and effect




Use scenario
Include or exclude that scenario from the comparison.


Scenario name
Unique nonempty label for plots, tables and the population to carry forward.


Population history
Constant keeps initial counts. Temporary change uses target counts from Start through End, inclusive, then returns to initial counts. Permanent change switches to target counts at Start. Linear change interpolates from initial counts at Start to target counts at End, then retains the target.


Target males; Target females
Sex-specific census counts during or after the change. At least two of each sex; combined count at most 500. Constant histories ignore these targets.


Change starts (gen); Change ends (gen)
Whole generations within the run, with Start no later than End. Constant ignores these dates; Permanent uses Start for the switch.


Mutation-rate multiplier
Multiplies the shared mutation rate for this scenario; 1 means unchanged, 0 means no mutation. The control allows 0-100.



The teaching defaults include Constant; Mild bottleneck (20 males and 20 females, generations 10-20); Expansion (80 of each sex from generation 12); Gradual decline (to 20 of each sex from generation 8 to 30); and Severe bottleneck (8 of each sex, generations 10-20). All start from 40 males and 40 females. Loading another preset changes these values.


Reading historical outputs and choosing a population







Control or output
Interpretation




Plot level / chromosome
Genome combines within-chromosome information; it does not estimate LD between chromosomes. Choose one chromosome for a focused comparison.


Show generation 0 (initial)
Adds the founder comparison. It helps distinguish sampling LD from LD accumulated during the history.


Plot population counts
Choose total animals, males or females. A return to the initial count does not restore alleles already lost.


Frequency view
ALT-allele frequency is the frequency p of allele 1. MAF is min(p, 1-p), so a common ALT allele can have low MAF.


Measure
Expected heterozygosity averages 2p(1-p); mean MAF averages minor frequencies; segregating fraction is the fraction with 0 < p < 1; fixed SNPs counts sites at p = 0 or 1.


Per-chromosome panels
Select LD decay, allele frequency or diversity for individual chromosome panels. These panels describe replicate 1.


Chromosome; Example SNP
Choose one marker for its allele-frequency trajectory in replicate 1. One trajectory is an illustration, not a replicate average.


Summary measure; Compare scenarios with
Select the metric and baseline for replicate summaries. Differences are scenario minus baseline, paired within replicate. Historical paired intervals are pointwise and not adjusted for multiple comparisons.


History to use in the base population
Choose the final scenario whose genome you want to carry forward. Check the same label after importing into Base population.


CSV table; Figure to export; Final population for phased VCF
Select which result to download. CSV contains tables, PNG contains a figure, and VCF contains phased marker genotypes. The full-population download retains the information needed by the next module.



LD decay reports phased haplotype r-squared: r-squared = (pAB - pA*pB)^2 / [pA(1-pA)pB(1-pB)]. Fixed sites have no defined correlation and are excluded. Pair distances use cM. Genome means weight sampled chromosome pairs to account for different sampling fractions. Nearby sites often show stronger LD, but individual bins need not follow a perfectly smooth curve or a fixed scenario ranking.
The LD decay and genetic diversity tabs show replicate means. Allele-frequency plots, individual trajectories, per-chromosome panels and the genome transferred to Base population use replicate 1. Downloads of replicate summaries retain all runs. A historical run and a recent breeding run use different definitions of a replicate; see Section 10.

title: User manual
section: 3. Base population: construction and genetic architecture
text:
3. Base population: construction and genetic architecture
Base animals are sampled from the final genome of the chosen historical scenario. For each chromosome, a complete paternal haplotype is sampled from the historical male pool and a maternal haplotype from the female pool, with replacement. This retains within-chromosome LD but does not reproduce the full historical genealogy. Year classes specify initial ages; they do not simulate past selection between those classes.
The module chooses segregating marker sites as major and minor quantitative trait loci (QTL). Effects are additive. Marker dosages and locus effects determine true breeding values (TBVs). The base sample is calibrated to the requested genetic covariance; major and background components are constructed orthogonally in that combined sample. The major-locus inherited effects include an LD correction. Conditional component effects and inherited locus effects therefore need not be numerically identical.
Without reaction norms, phenotype = TBV + residual. For trait j, residual variance Ve_j = Va_j*(1-h2_j)/h2_j. Residuals are independent across traits in their target covariance. Genetic and residual components are calibrated separately in the base sample; their realized cross-covariance need not be exactly zero. Exact target genetic covariance applies to all base animals together, not necessarily each herd or age class. It does not guarantee exact covariance or heritability in every small subgroup.

Population and trait parameters








Control
Starting value / options
Meaning and effect




Choose a case; Generate teaching case
B1-B7
Generates the selected prepared architecture using the selected historical genome, 80 animals and seed 2026. It changes several inputs and resets EV fields; reload the intended objective afterwards.


Optional: import another Module 1 RDS
Full historical population
Upload the history downloaded from the first application. Loading a small teaching example replaces the current history.


Historical scenario
Available final histories
Choose the scenario used for chromosome sampling. Confirm the intended history before generating animals.


Starting configuration; Load year-class preset
One herd/year 0; four year classes; two herds/four classes
Loads the year-class table. Loading a preset and generating animals are separate actions.


Editable year classes (year relative to time 0)
year, males, females, herd
Each row is one birth-year and herd group. Year 0 means born at time 0; year -3 means age 3 at time 0. Counts are nonnegative integers; each row needs animals. Year must be -100 to 0; year/herd combinations must be unique. Total base size is at most 1,000, with at least two males and two females overall.


Traits
1-3
Number of biological traits. Use one additive variance and one heritability per trait, in trait order.


Additive variances
1 per trait
Positive additive genetic variances in squared trait units. A larger value gives more genetic variation.


Genetic correlation 1-2; Correlation 1-3; Correlation 2-3
0.4, 0, 0 in ordinary controls
Correlations determine covariance: Cov(j,k) = rg(j,k)sqrt(Va_jVa_k). Only relevant pairs are used. For three traits, individually valid correlations may jointly produce an invalid matrix; the whole covariance matrix must be positive definite.


Trait heritabilities
0.3 per trait
Values strictly between 0 and 1. They determine residual variance. Increasing h2 while retaining Va reduces residual variation; it does not increase Va. With reaction norms, h2 refers to x = 0.


Number of major QTL
2; 1-5
Number of sampled large-component loci. A small number cannot represent every covariance structure or share.


Major-QTL share of total Vg (%)
15; 1-90
Share of the sum of genetic variances, not a guarantee for each trait. With reaction norms this share refers to intercept and slope coefficients together, not every environment. Infeasible combinations are rejected.


Minor-effect QTL
30; 3-1,000
Number of background loci, distinct from major loci. Enough eligible segregating markers and sample rank are required. With reaction norms there must be at least twice as many minor QTL as biological traits.


Min base MAF
0.01
Filters sites eligible to become QTL in the sampled base. This is separate from the historical initial-MAF setting and the genomic prediction panel filter.


Random seed; Generate base population
2026
Generates animals and effects from the currently displayed settings. Generating again replaces the current base.



Prepared examples: B1 uses one trait with h2 = 0.10; B2 uses h2 = 0.60. B3, B4 and B5 use two traits with h2 = 0.30 and genetic correlations +0.60, 0 and -0.60. B6 and B7 use one trait with reaction norms, h2 = 0.30, and slope/intercept variance ratios 0.20 and 0.80. Their additive variances are 1. Prepared cases are alternatives, not successive stages of one population.


Base outputs and display controls
Overview shows cohort counts and marker variation. In QTL positions & effects, Trait to plot and Chromosome select the displayed locus effects. The major table distinguishes conditional major effects from inherited effects. Covariance & scaling compares requested and realized covariance and the variance decomposition. Traits & cohorts uses its Trait selector for TBV distributions, phenotype-versus-TBV plots and cohort means. The biological-trait selector in Reaction norms chooses the reaction-norm outputs.
The full base-population download preserves animals, phased genomes, effects, phenotypes, ages and the saved objective. Animal, QTL, covariance and reaction-norm table downloads are useful for inspection but are not replacements for the full base transfer. Save results before generating another case.

title: User manual
text:
4. Economic objectives and correlated response
For the two-trait B3-B5 examples, open BV and economic values. An animal’s breeding value describes inherited merit in trait units. An economic value (EV) assigns a weight to a trait. Changing EVs changes the objective and ranking without changing the animals, their BVs or their covariance.
The objective is H = EV1BV1 + EV2BV2. The example objectives are E1 (1,1), E2 (1,0), E3 (2,1) and E4 (1,-1). Negative weights favour a reduction in that trait. Weights depend on trait units: a weight of 2 is not meaningful without knowing the scale. Multiplying all weights by the same positive constant preserves ranking but rescales numerical objective gain.







Control
Meaning and effect




Economic objective examples; Load EV example
Loads one of E1-E4 into the two EV fields. It does not create new animals.


EV for Trait1; EV for Trait2
Numerical weights. At least one must be nonzero.


Candidates selected (%)
5-50%, initially 20%. Rounds up to a whole number of selected candidates. Lower fractions generally imply stronger selection. This controls the base geometry demonstration, not the later schedule’s parent counts.


Rank candidates using
True BV objective demonstrates selection with perfect genetic information. Phenotype weighted by EVs demonstrates mass selection with residual noise.


Use these EVs in Module 3
Saves the objective with the current base. Download the full base after saving, then check the imported selection weights in Current population. Existing breeding results require a new run to change.



The ellipse is a 95% normal-theory genetic distribution contour centred on the sample mean. It is not a confidence interval for the mean and does not promise exactly 95% empirical coverage. Equal-merit lines describe combinations with equal H. The EV arrow shows objective direction; the expected genetic-shift arrow depends on genetic covariance. In general the two directions differ.
For multivariate normal truncation selection, expected selected-candidate shift = iGw / sqrt(w’ C w). Here G is additive covariance, w is the EV vector, i is normal-theory selection intensity for the selected fraction, and C is G for true-BV ranking or G + R for phenotype ranking. The observed shift is the actual selected candidates’ mean BV minus the full candidate mean. Finite samples can differ from the expectation. Neither shift is a simulated offspring response; offspring response comes from reproduction in Current population.

title: User manual
text:
5. Genotype by environment interaction
When genetic reaction norms are enabled, genetic value for animal i at environment x is g_i(x) = a_i + b_i*x. Both the intercept a_i and sensitivity b_i are inherited from the same locus architecture. Phenotype additionally contains a shared environmental mean slope times x and a residual. Changing a common environmental mean does not itself create genetic re-ranking.








Control
Starting value / options
Meaning and effect




Enable genetic reaction norms (G×E)
Off
Adds inherited genetic slopes to each biological trait.


Genetic slope variance / intercept variance
0.20; 0.01-1 in the control
Multiplies the reference genetic covariance for slope covariance. Larger values usually make genetic sensitivity and re-ranking more pronounced.


Genetic correlation: intercept vs slope
0; -0.95 to 0.95
Association between inherited merit at x = 0 and inherited sensitivity. Cross-covariance is rhosqrt(ratio)G0.


Evaluation environments
5; 2-15
Number of evenly spaced x values for assigning one observation environment per base animal, approximately balanced over the whole base. It is not repeated measurements on every base animal.


Environmental gradient: minimum; Environmental gradient: maximum
-1; +1
Limits of the evaluation grid. Minimum must be less than maximum, and the range must contain reference x = 0.


Fixed environmental mean slope
0
Shared change in phenotypic mean per unit x, separate from genetic slopes.


Biological trait
Display selector
Chooses the reaction norms, variances and re-ranking summary to inspect.



Reference covariance G0 applies to genetic intercepts at x = 0. Slope covariance is ratioG0. For one trait, genetic variance at x is Va + 2xCov(a,b) + x^2Vb. Residual variance remains constant along x, so heritability can vary between environments. The entered h2 is the reference value, not a universal value across the gradient.
Crossing genetic curves show re-ranking. The theoretical genetic correlation between x and z uses covariance Va + (x+z)Cov(a,b) + xz*Vb divided by the two genetic standard deviations. A realized rank correlation among a finite sample is a different statistic and need not equal that Pearson genetic correlation.
The breeding application maps each herd to a named environment and numerical x. Names such as Hot or Cool do not determine quality; x is a defined covariate. Base observations keep their original observed x. New offspring receive their birth herd’s x. The current model creates one phenotypic record per animal, not longitudinal repeated measurements. A single herd at x = 0 does not demonstrate selection across contrasting environments. The recent G×E plots also summarize genetic merit at x = -1 and +1, which should be interpreted relative to the chosen gradient.

title: User manual
section: 6. Current population: the yearly breeding cycle
text:
6. Current population: the yearly breeding cycle
Use Optional: import another base RDS to upload the full base population and confirm its historical source, cohorts and selection weights. The locus effects and base genotype centres are frozen. Each year the model identifies animals within reproductive-age limits, selects usable phenotypic records, predicts candidate merit, selects parents, chooses matings within capacity, and generates offspring by chromosome recombination. Offspring TBVs are reconstructed from their inherited loci; effects are not rescaled to force a desired gain or variance each year.
Animal cohorts overlap: a parent can breed in several years while age-eligible. There is no explicit mortality, survival selection, fertility failure, disease process or migration. Animals outside reproductive ages remain in recorded data but cannot become parents. Recent offspring do not receive new mutations in this model. Offspring phenotypes add residual noise to inherited genetic value, plus the known environmental mean when reaction norms are active.

Prepared programmes and basic controls








Control
Starting value / options
Meaning and effect




Choose a programme; Load programme settings
P1-P5 or young-candidate benchmark
P1 mass selection, P2 pedigree BLUP and P3 GBLUP each use four sires. P4 compares all three with four sires; P5 compares them with eight. These plans retain the imported base and saved objective and load 12 years, 20 offspring per herd/year and five replicates.


Workshop default: BLUP versus GBLUP (young candidates)
Prepared workshop case
Replaces the previous base with a prepared one-trait population containing recorded relatives. Uses 6 years, 80 births/year, four age-1 sires, 80 regular dams aged 1-4, no MOET, random mating, 100% phenotyping/genotyping, and own-record availability at age 2. It is not a continuation of B5.


Load teaching example
Alternative initial population
Replaces your imported population. Do not use it when you intend to retain the base you just constructed.


Beginner workshop view
Off
Simplifies the display and selects mass selection. It does not replace the need to apply a plan.


Simple teaching plan: Breeding years; Offspring per herd/year; Selected sires per herd
4; 20; 4
Apply simple plan uses one regular dam per offspring, no MOET, random mating and reproductive ages 1-10. Edits take effect after Apply simple plan, which clears earlier results. The simplified years control allows 1-8.


Selection index weights by trait
Imported EVs, or 1
One weight per biological trait, in order. At least one nonzero. Used for ranking and the true objective; compare gains only under compatible weights and scales.


Compare selection strategies
Mass selection, Pedigree BLUP, GBLUP, Single-step GBLUP, Oracle TBV
Choose one or more methods. Their meanings and information requirements appear in Section 9.


Breeding years
4 in ordinary full controls
Years to simulate; the active schedule needs one row per year and herd. Loading a named programme changes this value.


Random seed; Independent breeding replicates (paired by seed)
2026; 5
Starts each method from the same fixed imported base within each replicate. Up to 100 replicates. Selection changes the later populations, so matching seeds does not make all later animals or random events identical.





Ages, herds and information settings








Control
Starting value / options
Meaning and effect




Minimum sire age; Maximum sire age
1; 10
Inclusive age range in breeding years for male candidates. Age = current breeding year - birth year.


Minimum dam age; Maximum dam age
1; 10
Inclusive age range for female candidates. Initial year classes must supply enough age-eligible animals.


Sire availability
Within herd; Across herds
Whether male candidates can serve other herds. Dams remain within herd. Across-herd sire use shares per-sire offspring capacity across herds.


Mating design
Random; Low pedigree kinship
Random samples available selected parents. Low pedigree kinship samples candidate pairs and chooses a pair with low recorded coancestry, respecting capacities. It is a heuristic, not a global optimum or genomic optimum-contribution selection.


Male proportion of offspring
0.50; 0.10-0.90
Probability an offspring is male. Realized sex counts fluctuate; a 50% setting does not enforce equal counts.


Phenotyped offspring (%)
100; 20-100
Probability each new animal receives a phenotype, subject to measurement-age availability. It does not remove phenotypes already present in the imported base.


Age when own phenotype becomes available (years)
0
Records are withheld from evaluation until this age. Mass selection also needs an available own phenotype. Increasing the age creates young candidates lacking own records.


Genotyped offspring (%) - 100% for fair GBLUP benchmark
100; 0-100
Probability offspring genotypes are observed for prediction. All actual genomes are still transmitted biologically. Imported base animals are treated as genotyped. Pure GBLUP can use only genotyped candidates; incomplete genotyping can change the usable comparison group.


Reference phenotypes for BLUP / GBLUP / ssGBLUP
All recorded; Base only; Recent years; Base + recent
Chooses which existing recorded animals contribute phenotypes. Reference-herd and phenotype-age restrictions also apply. Base only uses birth year no later than 0; Recent years uses birth years at least current year minus the window.


Recent reference window (years)
3
Birth-year window for the Recent years component, not simply the last three batches of newly measured records.


Reference herds (phenotypic records)
All imported herds
Filters phenotypic reference records. It does not remove animals from the biological population or automatically remove their observed genotypes.


Genomic-panel SNPs
500; 50-10,000 requested
Samples up to this many eligible segregating panel markers. Eligible base allele frequencies must be greater than 0.01 and less than 0.99; fewer eligible markers means a smaller actual panel. At least ten are required.


A22 blend into genomic G
0.10; 0.02-0.50
Stabilizes the marker relationship matrix: Gstar = (1-blend)G + blendA22. A22 is the pedigree relationship submatrix for genotyped animals. A larger blend gives more pedigree influence; it is not heritability.


Exclude known causal QTL from genomic marker panel
On
Removes simulated causal loci from the prediction panel. Prediction then relies on linked marker information rather than direct observation of the causal sites. Turning it off changes the information scenario.


Herd → user-named environment and reaction norm x
herd, environment, x
One mapping row per herd. Environment is a user label; x is the numerical target for genetic merit and new observations. With no reaction norms, genetic slopes are zero.



Keep population, candidate group, recorded information, objective, selected-parent numbers, births, reproductive ages, mating design and period fixed when isolating the effect of a prediction method. Always check usable candidate counts; identical control settings do not guarantee identical usable candidates when genotypes or own phenotypes are missing.

title: User manual
section: 7. Breeding schedule, parent numbers and MOET
text:
7. Breeding schedule, parent numbers and MOET
The active schedule, not the template fields, drives reproduction. Each row is one breeding year and herd. In the table, year and herd identify the row; numerical cells can be edited. Inspect both arithmetic capacity and age eligibility before running.







Schedule column / template control
Meaning




year; herd
Breeding year and herd. A row is required for every simulated combination.


offspring / Offspring/herd/year
Number of births required in that row. This is a fixed total, not a birth probability.


sires / Selected sires
Number of highest-ranking usable male candidates sought. Actual selected count cannot exceed available candidates; capacities must still support all births.


regular_dams / Selected regular dams
Highest-ranking conventional dams after the donor group is removed.


moet_dams / Selected MOET dams
Highest-ranking donor dams, selected before regular dams. The two female groups do not overlap within that row.


moet_pct / MOET offspring %
Fraction of total births assigned to donors. Donor births = round(offspring*percentage/100); remaining births are conventional.


sire_cap / Offspring/sire
Maximum offspring per selected sire in that year, shared across herds when sires are used across herds.


regular_cap / Offspring/regular dam
Maximum conventional offspring per selected dam for the row.


moet_cap / Offspring/MOET dam
Maximum donor offspring per selected MOET dam for the row.



MOET means multiple ovulation and embryo transfer. Here it is an offspring-number approximation: selected donors can contribute more offspring. The model does not simulate embryo physiology, recipient dams, transfer failures, costs or fertility. Increasing donor output can concentrate ancestry and change gain and inbreeding; neither response is forced.
For each row, selected sires times sire capacity must cover all births; regular dams times regular capacity must cover conventional births; and donor dams times donor capacity must cover donor births. These arithmetic conditions are necessary but not sufficient: eligible animals and method-specific information must also be available. Selecting more parents than exist does not create new candidates.







Action or planner control
Effect and caution




Create / reset yearly schedule
Rebuilds the schedule from current template values and overwrites table edits.


Apply template to all existing years
Copies current template values into existing rows. Merely changing template fields does not update the active table.


Fix mating capacity in schedule
Adjusts selected-dam counts or sire capacity to address arithmetic shortfalls. It does not create eligible animals or alter the imported base or requested births.


Extend / trim years (keep edits)
Resizes the schedule to the requested period while retaining applicable edited rows. Recheck capacity afterwards.


Illustrative 15-year dairy template
Loads a larger example. It is illustrative and can be slow; it does not guarantee feasible age structure or a calibrated dairy herd.


Save schedule CSV; Import edited schedule CSV
Downloads or uploads the yearly plan. Reinspect the active schedule after import.


Target fraction of candidates selected
Initially 0.70, range 0.10-1. Used by the feasibility planner, not a replacement for actual schedule parent counts. Lower fractions imply needing more candidates for a fixed number selected.


Dairy feasibility planner
Year 1 uses actual imported ages and sexes. Later projections use planned births and assume no mortality. It is an approximation and does not modify the population.


Add base founders to meet Year 1 target
Explicitly adds sampled whole-chromosome founders to reproductive-age classes. This changes the starting population and assumes new unrelated founders; it is not pedigree development through earlier breeding. Use only as a deliberate new scenario. Save expanded base downloads the changed population.



If a run reports a shortfall, identify the year, herd, sex, recording requirement and capacity involved. Correct the biological plan rather than interpreting a failed run as a scientific result. For a matched comparison, make any intentional correction before running every method.

title: User manual
text:
8. Breeding outputs and display parameters







Output or control
How to interpret it




Overview
Check imported animals, genome, run configuration and cohort sizes before interpreting outcomes.


Genetic trait
Selects the trait’s genetic mean and variance. With multiple traits inspect all trait responses as well as the weighted objective.


Genetic gain
Changes in true genetic values of newborn cohorts relative to the imported baseline. The ordinary baseline is the combined base; the prepared genomic case uses its configured youngest-base reference.


Annual genetic gain (index)
(Final mean true objective - initial baseline mean true objective) / number of breeding years. This is endpoint average gain per year, not a fitted trend slope or a per-generation response.


Remaining genetic variance
Sample variance of TBV in the displayed cohort. Selection, drift, segregation and changing relationships can alter it; it is not held at its initial target.


Pedigree inbreeding F
F_i = A_ii - 1, computed from recorded parents. Ordinary sampled founders have F = 0 by convention; historical inbreeding is not reconstructed by that pedigree. A supplied recorded pedigree contributes relationships.


Annualized pedigree inbreeding rate, %
100*[1 - ((1-F_final)/(1-F_initial))^(1/years)]. This is an annual change relative to remaining non-inbred proportion; it is not F divided by years or a rate per generation.


Heterozygosity
Observed fraction of heterozygous inherited SNP genotypes per animal, averaged over the cohort. Different from historical expected heterozygosity 2p(1-p), and different from pedigree F.


Candidate group
Young candidates without an own record; All eligible candidates; Sire candidates. These are distinct groups and can have different accuracies.


Selection accuracy
Pre-selection sample correlation between true target-environment genetic objective and the method’s selection criterion among candidates with finite scores. For BLUP methods the criterion is predicted genetic merit; for mass selection it is weighted phenotype.


Young-candidate accuracy
Restricts to candidates younger than own-phenotype availability age. It is not the same as every animal with a missing own record. At age setting 0 this group is empty.


Candidate statistics
Reports age-eligible and usable/genotyped candidates, reference records and selected parents. Correlation is unavailable if there are too few usable candidates or negligible variation; unavailable does not mean zero.


Generation interval
Average actual parental age at offspring birth, weighted by the actual matings/offspring. Combined interval averages sire and dam contributions; separate sire and dam intervals can differ.


Biological trait in Reaction norm G×E
Selects environment-specific genetic predictions and cohort response. Genetic values use inherited intercept plus x times slope.


Selection scenario in Pedigree & animals
Chooses which method’s stored individual animals and mating records to inspect. Individual details are retained for replicate 1.


Compare; Error bars for method comparison
Chooses the outcome and SE, SD, 95% interval or no band in replicate comparison. These are statistical display choices and do not change simulated biology.



Accuracy uses TBVs only to evaluate predictions. The BLUP prediction solver does not use candidate TBVs as observations. Oracle TBV is the explicitly labelled exception for a perfect-information demonstration. These realized correlations are simulation diagnostics, not cross-validation results from an external dataset. Replicate accuracy summaries average valid year/herd correlations; they are not one pooled correlation of all animals.
Save files & validation offers full-population results, trends, reference/accuracy tables, individual predictions, animal/pedigree records, matings, marker-panel information, replicate summaries and paired tests. Full individual genomes and records are retained for replicate 1 of each method; trends and statistical summaries cover all replicates. Use the individual-prediction CSV to inspect candidate TBVs, EBVs, age, selection and record use. Download your results before replacing a run.

title: User manual
text:
9. Selection and prediction methods

Mass selection and Oracle TBV
Mass selection ranks candidates using the EV-weighted sum of their own phenotypes. An animal without usable own phenotypes, or younger than the phenotype-availability age, cannot receive a usable mass-selection score. Environmental and residual variation can make phenotype rank differ from genetic rank. It does not use pedigree to improve predictions.
Oracle TBV ranks on the true EV-weighted genetic value at the target environment. It is a perfect-information teaching reference. Real breeders do not know TBVs. Do not interpret it as a practical prediction method.


Pedigree BLUP
Pedigree BLUP combines available phenotypes with additive pedigree relationships A. A has founder diagonal 1, offspring relationships equal to the average of parental relationships, and offspring F equal to half the relationship between sire and dam. Unknown founders are unrelated in the recorded pedigree, even when their sampled genomes share historical ancestry.
For a trait without G×E, genetic covariance between individuals i and j is A_ijVa. The predictor is the covariance-based BLUP expression: predicted candidate merit = Cov(candidate, recorded animals)[Cov(recorded genetic values) + Ve*I]^-1*(recorded phenotypes - known fixed mean). Genetic and residual parameters come from the base setup; they are not estimated by fitting variance components to each run. Known simulated fixed environmental means are subtracted rather than estimated as unknown herd or year effects. A small numerical stabilizer is used in solving.


GBLUP and single-step GBLUP
GBLUP uses marker-based realized relationships. Marker dosage is 0, 1 or 2; W centres dosage at 2p using base-panel allele frequencies, which remain fixed over years. The genomic relationship matrix is G = W*W’ / sum[2p(1-p)]. It is blended toward the corresponding pedigree block A22 for numerical stability.
Pure GBLUP uses genotyped reference animals and genotyped candidates only. Non-genotyped candidates do not receive a hidden pedigree fallback. For a fair BLUP/GBLUP information comparison use 100% candidate genotyping, the same phenotypic reference information and matched breeding settings. Marker information is useful only to the extent that it informs relevant genetic relationships and linked effects; a random tiny population or sparse panel need not show a strong advantage.
Single-step GBLUP combines pedigree and observed genomic information in one relationship matrix H. In inverse form, H^-1 equals A^-1 plus a genotyped-animal block containing Gstar^-1 - A22^-1. Thus it can connect genotyped and non-genotyped animals through pedigree. The implementation uses an algebraically equivalent covariance form. The genotyping fraction controls which animals enter the genomic block; the reference policy controls which phenotypes are used. These are separate choices.


Multiple traits and reaction-norm prediction
Each biological trait is predicted separately, then trait predictions are combined with EV weights. The simulation generates genetic correlations between biological traits, but prediction does not use a full multi-trait BLUP that borrows phenotypic information between those traits.
With reaction norms, each trait has a jointly modelled genetic intercept and slope. Covariance of observed genetic records at x_i and x_j is S_ij*[Va + Cov(a,b)(x_i+x_j) + Vbx_i*x_j], where S is A, blended G or H. Candidate prediction uses the corresponding covariance at its target x. This is a linear genetic random-regression model per biological trait. Residual variance is constant along x; no nonlinear reaction norm or residual G×E is fitted.

title: User manual
text:
10. Replicates, uncertainty and fair comparisons
Historical replicates redraw founders. Within a historical replicate, the demographic scenarios share the founder genome. Only replicate 1 supplies the genome carried forward. Recent breeding replicates instead share one fixed imported base and frozen architecture, and repeat selection and reproduction with different seeds. Their uncertainty is conditional on that base; it does not include variation over newly generated historical populations.
SD describes run-to-run variation; SE describes uncertainty in an estimated mean. A 95% t interval is mean plus or minus t(0.975,n-1)*SE. With one valid replicate these quantities are unavailable. More replicates improve precision but do not correct a biased model, incomparable objectives or unmatched populations.
Recent method comparisons pair results by replicate. Differences are method A minus method B. Paired t tests use those differences and report Holm-adjusted p-values across pairwise method comparisons for the selected outcome. Confidence intervals remain ordinary pointwise intervals. Small numbers of replicates have little power for small effects; statistical significance is not the same as teaching or practical importance.
The workshop young-candidate case was designed to make genomic information informative before an own record becomes available. Inspect measured accuracy and gain, together with uncertainty and candidate counts. It is not a universal ranking of methods or evidence that GBLUP must reduce inbreeding. Relatedness, mating decisions, parental contributions and realized selection determine the inbreeding outcome.
The breeder equation gives a useful interpretation of response: annual gain is related to selection intensity, prediction accuracy, genetic standard deviation and generation interval. This simulation explicitly generates inheritance and matings; it does not set gain by substituting an assumed accuracy into that equation. Repeated selection changes variance and relationships, so a simple constant-parameter prediction need not track every year.

title: User manual
text:
11. Practical limitations and troubleshooting
If LD is absent, check for segregating markers, the initial frequency mode, mutation, distance bins and sampled-pair counts. All-ancestral founders without mutation cannot create polymorphism. If a bin has very few pairs, interpret it cautiously. A bottleneck can increase LD while reducing diversity; population-size recovery need not restore lost variation.
If base generation fails, check positive variances, a positive-definite correlation matrix, enough segregating loci passing MAF, enough animals and an attainable major-QTL share. Extreme shares or dependent loci can be infeasible. Changing a seed is a new realization; keep it fixed when the point is to isolate one parameter.
If a breeding run fails, check the active schedule, parent ages, usable own records/genotypes, reference-herd/window filters and mating capacities. Pure GBLUP needs at least three genotyped phenotypic reference animals in each evaluation year. A capacity repair does not create candidates. Importing another base or adding founders changes the comparison and should be documented as a new scenario.
If the genomic teaching case replaces your population, return to your saved full base before continuing the broader exercise. If the selection weights differ after transfer, save the intended EVs in Base population, download the full base again and re-import it. Record the base identity, objective, period, methods, settings and replicate count alongside your conclusions.
Large populations, many years, many markers and many replicates can make prediction slow. Relationship matrices grow with all retained animals. Start with a small prepared plan. The larger dairy template is not a guarantee that a browser-hosted session can complete that workload.
ADAM-Edu uses simplified additive inheritance, finite marker maps, known variance parameters and known environmental means. It does not implement dominance, epistasis, full multi-trait prediction, commercial economic optimisation, complete livestock demography or a production breeding evaluation. Use it to investigate mechanisms, compare controlled scenarios and discuss what additional evidence a real breeding decision would require.

title: User manual
text:
12. Glossary







Term
Meaning




SNP; QTL
A biallelic marker site; a locus assigned an effect on a quantitative trait. Some SNPs act as simulated causal QTL.


Haplotype; genotype dosage
Alleles along one chromosome copy; count of allele 1 across the two copies at a site.


LD; MAF
Association between alleles at different loci; frequency of the less common allele at one locus.


TBV; EBV
True additive genetic value known by the simulator; estimated breeding value from available information.


Va; Ve; h2
Additive genetic variance; residual variance; Va/(Va+Ve) at the specified population/environment.


Genetic correlation
Standardized additive covariance between two traits or environmental expressions.


EV; H
Economic value or trait weight; the weighted true genetic objective. The same symbol H also commonly denotes the single-step relationship matrix; the context distinguishes them.


A; G; H relationship matrices
Pedigree, genomic and combined single-step additive relationships. Genetic covariance G in the base module is a trait covariance matrix, distinct from genomic relationship G.


Reference population
Animals whose usable phenotypic records contribute to prediction, subject to selected filters.


Candidate; selected parent
An eligible animal evaluated before selection; an animal actually chosen for reproduction.


Cohort; generation interval
Animals born in one breeding year; average parental age at offspring birth. A breeding year is not a non-overlapping generation.


Inbreeding; heterozygosity
Recorded pedigree autozygosity expectation relative to its founders; proportion of heterozygous marker genotypes or its frequency-based expectation, as labelled.


Reaction norm; G×E
Genetic value expressed as a function of environment; inherited differences in environmental sensitivity that can change relative performance.


MOET
Multiple ovulation and embryo transfer, approximated here through selected donor dams and offspring capacities.

ADAM-Edu is an interactive teaching tool for animal breeding and quantitative genetics. Explore how population history, trait relationships, selection and reproduction affect genetic change.

Before the workshop
You need only a computer, a modern web browser and internet access. No installation, R, programming or account is needed. Open the three applications below to check access, and save the manual and practical PDFs. Any reliable internet connection works.
The practical starts with LD and history, then base traits and economic values. Its main breeding task compares prediction methods for young candidates and explores donor reproduction. Finish by planning a teaching activity.

title: 30-minute practical
text:
Download the practical (PDF)
Explore LD, connect trait relationships to a breeding objective, then make a breeding decision using prediction accuracy, gain and diversity. Predict before looking at a result.

title: 30-minute practical
text:
0-4 minutes: historical population and LD
Open Historical population. Inspect Population history, LD decay and Genetic diversity for Constant, Mild bottleneck and Severe bottleneck. Use the prepared LD figure on the workshop page if a new comparison is still running. Compare short and long genetic distances and expected heterozygosity. These prepared curves are one simulated replicate, not replicate means.

Does LD decrease with distance? Is one history highest in every bin?
Why can population numbers recover without restoring lost genetic variation?

Choose Mild bottleneck and download the full historical population. If needed, use the prepared historical population on the workshop page instead; it includes the LD results.

title: 30-minute practical
section: 4-8 minutes: base population and breeding objective
text:
4-8 minutes: base population and breeding objective
Open Base population and upload that full history. Select the Mild bottleneck final scenario, choose B5 (negative genetic correlation) and click Generate teaching case. Inspect phenotype versus TBV. In BV and economic values, use true-BV ranking and 20% selected. Compare E2 (1,0) with E3 (2,1), without regenerating the animals. Save E3 with Use these EVs in Module 3 and download the full base for a later extended lesson.

Why can selection for Trait1 change Trait2? Which direction is favourable for each trait?
Changing economic values changes the objective and ranking. Does it change the animals’ underlying breeding values?

The next task deliberately uses a separate prepared one-trait population. It is not a numerical continuation of B5. This gives both prediction methods the same controlled starting point.

title: 30-minute practical
section: 8-25 minutes: breeding programme and a reproductive decision
text:
8-25 minutes: breeding programme and a reproductive decision
Run A: information for young candidates. Open Current population. Choose Workshop default: BLUP versus GBLUP (young candidates), then Load programme settings. Alternatively upload the prepared breeding population from the workshop page, then load the workshop default. Check: 6 years, 80 births/year, 4 age-1 sires, 80 regular dams aged 1-4, no MOET, 5 replicates and seed 2026. Keep Pedigree BLUP and GBLUP selected. Click Run breeding comparison once.
Young candidates have no own phenotype before age 2; their recorded relatives provide information. Both methods use the same available phenotypes, base, candidate numbers, selected-parent counts and reproductive settings. GBLUP additionally uses genomic relationships. Select young-candidate accuracy when inspecting Selection accuracy. It is the measured correlation between TBV and EBV before selection, not an assumed label.
Record both methods’ realized accuracy, annual genetic gain, annual inbreeding rate and generation interval. Use the measured-comparison table in Workshop guide and inspect the curves and replicate uncertainty. Do not expect identical numbers in every run.
Run B: donor reproduction. Record A first. In Breeding schedule & selection change only the template: regular dams 40, MOET dams 4, MOET offspring share 50%, maximum offspring per MOET dam 10. Keep 80 total offspring, 4 sires and all other A settings. Apply the template to all years, check the table, then run again. This compares 40 conventional births plus 40 donor births with A’s 80 conventional births. MOET here approximates extra offspring from selected donor dams; it does not model recipients or embryo physiology.

How much higher are realized accuracy and gain with genomic information in A? Why does limited own information matter?
How does B change gain and parental contributions? Does concentrating births in donor families change inbreeding?
Would you recommend B from gain alone? Compare diversity and generation interval. MOET does not automatically shorten the interval or lower inbreeding.

If runs are slow, use the prepared reference table for A and discuss the predicted trade-off in B. Label a prediction clearly; do not present it as an observed result. Avoid repeated clicks or larger settings during the timed session.

title: 30-minute practical
text:
25-30 minutes: your teaching activity
Choose LD, heritability, correlated response, economic objectives, GxE, prediction or reproduction as your learning goal. State one input to change, one outcome to interpret and the prediction students must make first. Explain one model limitation and one breeding decision that requires more information than these simulations provide.

title: 30-minute practical
text:
Results to record
Record an LD observation, a diversity observation, the E2/E3 correlated response, and A/B settings with method, seed and replicate count. For each breeding method record accuracy, gain, inbreeding rate and generation interval. Compare A and B using the same base, units and time period. Higher GBLUP accuracy does not guarantee lower inbreeding.

title: Current population
text:
For the practical, load the prepared workshop default and compare BLUP with GBLUP for young candidates. Record accuracy, gain, inbreeding and generation interval, then compare a donor reproduction plan. Extended P1-P5 lessons can retain a base imported from Base population.
